```{r}
# ============================================================
# Model Comparison: Friedman Test and Nemenyi Post-Hoc Test
# ============================================================
# Cross-validation folds are treated as repeated measures across models.
# The Nemenyi post-hoc test is performed only when the Friedman test is significant.

run_model_comparison <- function(path) {

  # Read the fold-level AUC results exported from Python
  cv <- read.csv(
    path,
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = 1
  )

  mat <- as.matrix(cv)

  cat("\n---", basename(path), "---\n")

  # Report mean AUC for each model
  print(round(colMeans(mat), 4))

  # Friedman test across the four models
  ft <- friedman.test(mat)
  print(ft)

  # Perform post-hoc comparisons only when the omnibus test is significant
  if (ft$p.value < 0.05) {
    cat("\nPost-hoc Nemenyi test:\n")
    print(frdAllPairsNemenyiTest(mat))
  } else {
    cat("\nFriedman test not significant; no post-hoc test performed.\n")
  }
}

# Run the comparison independently for each dataset
run_model_comparison(
  here("data", "taiwan_cv_auc.csv")
)

run_model_comparison(
  here("data", "german_cv_auc.csv")
)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================
# RQ1: Explanation-Method Concordance
# Kendall's W and Pairwise Spearman Rank Correlations
# ============================================================
# Kendall's W assesses overall agreement when three explanation methods are
# available. Pairwise Spearman correlations show agreement between individual
# explanation-method pairs.

run_concordance <- function(path) {

  # Read feature-level importance values exported from Python
  imp <- read.csv(
    path,
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = 1
  )

  cat("\n---", basename(path), "---\n")

  models <- c(
    "Logistic Regression",
    "XGBoost",
    "TensorFlow NN",
    "PyTorch NN"
  )

  for (m in models) {

    # Identify the explanation-method columns belonging to the current model
    cols <- grep(
      paste0("^", m, "__"),
      colnames(imp),
      value = TRUE
    )

    # Kendall's W is calculated where three explanation methods are available
    if (length(cols) >= 3) {
      cat(sprintf("\n%s - three-way Kendall's W:\n", m))

      print(
        KendallW(
          imp[, cols],
          correct = TRUE,
          test = TRUE
        )
      )
    }

    # Calculate pairwise Spearman rank correlations where at least two
    # explanation methods are available
    if (length(cols) >= 2) {
      cat(sprintf("\n%s - pairwise Spearman correlations:\n", m))

      cm <- cor(
        imp[, cols],
        method = "spearman"
      )

      # Remove the model prefix so only explanation-method names are shown
      short <- sub(
        paste0("^", m, "__"),
        "",
        colnames(cm)
      )

      dimnames(cm) <- list(short, short)

      print(round(cm, 3))
    }
  }
}

run_concordance(
  here("data", "taiwan_xai_importance.csv")
)

run_concordance(
  here("data", "german_xai_importance.csv")
)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================
# RQ2: TensorFlow and PyTorch Framework Comparison
# Paired Wilcoxon Tests Across Matched Seeds
# ============================================================
# Feature-level SHAP values are compared between TensorFlow and PyTorch using
# paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across the ten matched random seeds.
# Feature-level p values are adjusted using the Bonferroni correction.
#
# Training outcomes are compared using the same paired-seed design.
# Final validation loss is retained as an implementation diagnostic rather
# than a strictly like-for-like framework measure.

run_rq2 <- function(shap_path, train_path) {

  cat("\n===", basename(shap_path), "===\n")

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Match TensorFlow and PyTorch Observations by Seed
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  pair_by_seed <- function(data, value_col) {

    tf <- data[
      data$framework == "TensorFlow",
      c("seed", value_col)
    ]

    pt <- data[
      data$framework == "PyTorch",
      c("seed", value_col)
    ]

    # Each framework should contain one observation per seed
    if (anyDuplicated(tf$seed) || anyDuplicated(pt$seed)) {
      stop("Duplicate seed values found in paired RQ2 data.")
    }

    # Both frameworks must contain the same set of seeds
    if (!setequal(tf$seed, pt$seed)) {
      stop("TensorFlow and PyTorch seed values do not match.")
    }

    names(tf)[2] <- "TensorFlow"
    names(pt)[2] <- "PyTorch"

    paired <- merge(
      tf,
      pt,
      by = "seed"
    )

    paired[order(paired$seed), ]
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Feature-Level SHAP Comparison
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  shap_data <- read.csv(
    shap_path,
    check.names = FALSE
  )

  features <- unique(shap_data$feature)

  pvals <- sapply(features, function(feature_name) {

    feature_data <- shap_data[
      shap_data$feature == feature_name,
    ]

    paired <- pair_by_seed(
      feature_data,
      "importance"
    )

    wilcox.test(
      paired$TensorFlow,
      paired$PyTorch,
      paired = TRUE
    )$p.value
  })

  # Bonferroni correction across feature-level tests
  padj <- p.adjust(
    pvals,
    method = "bonferroni"
  )

  results <- data.frame(
    feature = features,
    p = round(pvals, 4),
    p_bonf = round(padj, 4)
  )

  cat(
    "Features differing after Bonferroni correction:",
    sum(padj < 0.05),
    "of",
    length(features),
    "\n"
  )

  print(
    head(
      results[order(results$p_bonf), ],
      10
    )
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Training-Outcome Comparison
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  training_data <- read.csv(
    train_path,
    check.names = FALSE
  )

  training_metrics <- c(
    "test_auc",
    "epochs",
    "final_val_loss",
    "train_seconds"
  )

  for (metric in training_metrics) {

    paired <- pair_by_seed(
      training_data,
      metric
    )

    p_value <- wilcox.test(
      paired$TensorFlow,
      paired$PyTorch,
      paired = TRUE
    )$p.value

    cat(
      sprintf(
        "%-16s  TF %.4f  PyTorch %.4f  Wilcoxon p = %.4f\n",
        metric,
        mean(paired$TensorFlow),
        mean(paired$PyTorch),
        p_value
      )
    )
  }
}


# Run the framework comparison independently for each dataset
run_rq2(
  here("data", "taiwan_rq2_shap.csv"),
  here("data", "taiwan_rq2_training.csv")
)

run_rq2(
  here("data", "german_rq2_shap.csv"),
  here("data", "german_rq2_training.csv")
)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================
# RQ3: Demographic Outcome Disparity
# Four-Fifths Screening Criterion with Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
# ============================================================
# The favourable outcome is predicted non-default, coded as 0.
# The four-fifths ratio is the lowest favourable-outcome rate divided by
# the highest favourable-outcome rate across the groups being compared.
#
# A point estimate below 0.8 is treated as falling below the screening
# threshold, not as evidence of unlawful discrimination.
#
# Uncertainty is quantified using 2,000 nonparametric bootstrap resamples
# and percentile-based 95% confidence intervals.


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Four-Fifths Ratio
# ------------------------------------------------------------

four_fifths_ratio <- function(pred, group) {

  rates <- tapply(
    pred == 0,
    group,
    mean
  )

  rates <- rates[!is.na(rates)]

  if (length(rates) < 2) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }

  min(rates) / max(rates)
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# RQ3 Analysis
# ------------------------------------------------------------

run_rq3 <- function(
  pred_path,
  age_col,
  age_breaks,
  age_labels,
  male_code,
  models
) {

  cat("\n===", basename(pred_path), "===\n")

  # Read test-set predictions and demographic variables exported from Python
  d <- read.csv(
    pred_path,
    check.names = FALSE
  )

  # Reconstruct readable sex labels from the dataset-specific encoding
  d$SEX_label <- ifelse(
    d$SEX == male_code,
    "male",
    "female"
  )

  # Use the same age bands as the Python analysis and dissertation
  d$AGE_band <- cut(
    d[[age_col]],
    breaks = age_breaks,
    labels = age_labels
  )

  for (m in models) {

    for (attr in c("SEX_label", "AGE_band")) {

      group <- d[[attr]]

      # Four-fifths point estimate
      point <- four_fifths_ratio(
        d[[m]],
        group
      )

      # Nonparametric bootstrap confidence interval
      bootstrap_data <- data.frame(
        pred = d[[m]],
        group = group
      )

      bs <- boot(
        data = bootstrap_data,
        R = 2000,
        statistic = function(dat, i) {
          four_fifths_ratio(
            dat$pred[i],
            dat$group[i]
          )
        }
      )

      ci <- quantile(
        as.numeric(bs$t),
        probs = c(0.025, 0.975),
        na.rm = TRUE
      )

      flag <- ifelse(
        !is.na(point) && point < 0.8,
        "  <-- below 0.8 screening threshold",
        ""
      )

      cat(
        sprintf(
          "%-22s %-9s four-fifths ratio = %.3f  95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]%s\n",
          m,
          attr,
          point,
          ci[1],
          ci[2],
          flag
        )
      )
    }
  }
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Run RQ3 for Both Datasets
# ------------------------------------------------------------

models <- c(
  "Logistic_Regression",
  "XGBoost",
  "TensorFlow_NN",
  "PyTorch_NN"
)

run_rq3(
  pred_path = here("data", "taiwan_test_predictions.csv"),
  age_col = "AGE",
  age_breaks = c(20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 100),
  age_labels = c("21-30", "31-40", "41-50", "51-60", "61+"),
  male_code = 1,
  models = models
)

run_rq3(
  pred_path = here("data", "german_test_predictions.csv"),
  age_col = "Age",
  age_breaks = c(18, 25, 35, 45, 60, 100),
  age_labels = c("19-25", "26-35", "36-45", "46-60", "61+"),
  male_code = 0,
  models = models
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Demographic Attribution Comparison
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Inspect Taiwan demographic SHAP importance for descriptive comparison with
# the group-level outcome disparities reported above.

taiwan_importance <- read.csv(
  here("data", "taiwan_xai_importance.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = 1
)

cat("\nTaiwan demographic feature importance by model and explanation method:\n")

print(
  round(
    taiwan_importance[
      rownames(taiwan_importance) %in%
        c("SEX", "AGE", "EDUCATION", "MARRIAGE"),
    ],
    4
  )
)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================
# Figure 4.1: Cross-Validated AUC by Model and Dataset
# ============================================================
# Boxplots summarise the distribution of the five cross-validation fold AUC
# values for each model. Individual fold values are shown as plotted points.
# Fold-to-fold variability is greater for the German dataset, particularly
# for the PyTorch neural network.

cv_long <- function(path, dataset_label) {

  read.csv(
    here("data", path),
    check.names = FALSE
  ) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -fold,
      names_to = "model",
      values_to = "auc"
    ) |>
    transform(
      dataset = dataset_label
    )
}


# Combine the two datasets for a common figure
cv_all <- rbind(
  cv_long(
    "taiwan_cv_auc.csv",
    "Taiwan dataset"
  ),
  cv_long(
    "german_cv_auc.csv",
    "German dataset"
  )
)


# Keep model and dataset ordering consistent across panels
cv_all$model <- factor(
  cv_all$model,
  levels = c(
    "Logistic Regression",
    "XGBoost",
    "TensorFlow NN",
    "PyTorch NN"
  )
)

cv_all$dataset <- factor(
  cv_all$dataset,
  levels = c(
    "Taiwan dataset",
    "German dataset"
  )
)


# Create the cross-validation AUC comparison
p_cv <- ggplot(
  cv_all,
  aes(x = model, y = auc)
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "#8fbfbf",
    colour = "#20404a",
    width = 0.55,
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.08,
      height = 0,
      seed = 42
    ),
    shape = 21,
    fill = "#20404a",
    colour = "#20404a",
    size = 2.4
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0.50, 0.85, by = 0.05),
    minor_breaks = seq(0.50, 0.85, by = 0.025)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(0.50, 0.85)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ dataset) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Cross-validated AUC"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey88"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey93"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 20,
      hjust = 1
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 11
    ),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.4, "lines")
  )


# Save the figure to the repository image directory
ggsave(
  here("images", "fig_cv_auc.png"),
  plot = p_cv,
  width = 8,
  height = 4,
  dpi = 300,
  bg = "white"
)

print(p_cv)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================
```
```{r}
# Figure 4.3: Top Twelve XGBoost SHAP Features by Dataset
# ============================================================
# The twelve highest-ranked XGBoost features are shown for each dataset.
# Taiwan feature codes are replaced with descriptive labels for readability.
# Demographic attributes appearing within the top twelve are highlighted
# separately from the remaining behavioural and financial features.

demographic_features <- c(
  "AGE",
  "SEX",
  "EDUCATION",
  "MARRIAGE",
  "Age"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Readable Labels for Taiwan Features
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# German feature names are already descriptive, whereas the Taiwan dataset
# uses abbreviated feature codes.

taiwan_labels <- c(
  PAY_1 = "Repayment status, most recent",
  PAY_2 = "Repayment status, 1 month earlier",
  PAY_3 = "Repayment status, 2 months earlier",
  PAY_4 = "Repayment status, 3 months earlier",
  PAY_5 = "Repayment status, 4 months earlier",
  PAY_6 = "Repayment status, 5 months earlier",

  PAY_AMT1 = "Payment amount, most recent",
  PAY_AMT2 = "Payment amount, 1 month earlier",
  PAY_AMT3 = "Payment amount, 2 months earlier",
  PAY_AMT4 = "Payment amount, 3 months earlier",
  PAY_AMT5 = "Payment amount, 4 months earlier",
  PAY_AMT6 = "Payment amount, 5 months earlier",

  BILL_AMT1 = "Bill amount, most recent",
  BILL_AMT2 = "Bill amount, 1 month earlier",
  BILL_AMT3 = "Bill amount, 2 months earlier",
  BILL_AMT4 = "Bill amount, 3 months earlier",
  BILL_AMT5 = "Bill amount, 4 months earlier",
  BILL_AMT6 = "Bill amount, 5 months earlier",

  LIMIT_BAL = "Credit limit",
  EDUCATION = "Education",
  MARRIAGE = "Marital status",
  AGE = "Age",
  SEX = "Sex"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Extract Highest-Ranked XGBoost SHAP Features
# ------------------------------------------------------------

top_features <- function(path, dataset_label, n = 12) {

  read.csv(
    here("data", path),
    check.names = FALSE
  ) |>
    select(
      feature,
      imp = `XGBoost__SHAP`
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(imp)) |>
    slice_head(n = n) |>
    mutate(
      dataset = dataset_label,
      demographic = feature %in% demographic_features
    )
}


# Combine the top twelve features from both datasets
feat_all <- rbind(
  top_features(
    "taiwan_xai_importance.csv",
    "Taiwan dataset"
  ),
  top_features(
    "german_xai_importance.csv",
    "German dataset"
  )
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Relabel Taiwan Feature Codes
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Unmapped names are retained unchanged, which preserves the already-readable
# German feature names.

feat_all$feature <- ifelse(
  !is.na(taiwan_labels[feat_all$feature]),
  taiwan_labels[feat_all$feature],
  feat_all$feature
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Prepare Plot Ordering
# ------------------------------------------------------------

feat_all <- feat_all |>
  mutate(
    dataset = factor(
      dataset,
      levels = c(
        "Taiwan dataset",
        "German dataset"
      )
    ),
    row_id = paste(
      dataset,
      feature,
      sep = "___"
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(
    dataset,
    imp
  )

feat_all$row_id <- factor(
  feat_all$row_id,
  levels = feat_all$row_id
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Create Figure
# ------------------------------------------------------------

p_feat <- ggplot(
  feat_all,
  aes(
    x = imp,
    y = row_id,
    fill = demographic
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ dataset,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    labels = function(x) {
      sub("^.*___", "", x)
    }
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "FALSE" = "#8fbfbf",
      "TRUE" = "#c1666b"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "FALSE" = "Behavioural / financial",
      "TRUE" = "Demographic attribute"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean absolute SHAP value",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(
    base_size = 11
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 11
    ),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(
      1.4,
      "lines"
    )
  )


# Save the figure to the repository image directory
ggsave(
  here("images", "fig_top_features.png"),
  plot = p_feat,
  width = 9,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300,
  bg = "white"
)

print(p_feat)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================
# Figure 4.6: Taiwan Favourable-Outcome Rate by Age Band
# ============================================================
# This figure shows the favourable-outcome rate (predicted non-default)
# across the age bands used in the Taiwan fairness analysis. It provides
# a visual illustration of the age-related disparity discussed in the
# Results chapter.

pred <- read.csv(
  here("data", "taiwan_test_predictions.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Define Age Bands
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# These age bands match those used in the four-fifths analysis.

age_bands <- cut(
  pred$AGE,
  breaks = c(20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 100),
  labels = c("21-30", "31-40", "41-50", "51-60", "61+")
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Model Columns and Display Names
# ------------------------------------------------------------

model_cols <- c(
  "Logistic_Regression",
  "XGBoost",
  "TensorFlow_NN",
  "PyTorch_NN"
)

model_names <- c(
  "Logistic Regression",
  "XGBoost",
  "TensorFlow NN",
  "PyTorch NN"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate Favourable-Outcome Rates
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# A favourable outcome is predicted non-default, coded as class 0.

rate_df <- lapply(seq_along(model_cols), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    band = levels(age_bands),
    model = model_names[i],
    rate = tapply(
      pred[[model_cols[i]]] == 0,
      age_bands,
      mean
    )
  )
}) |> bind_rows()


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Set Plot Ordering
# ------------------------------------------------------------

rate_df$band <- factor(
  rate_df$band,
  levels = c("21-30", "31-40", "41-50", "51-60", "61+")
)

rate_df$model <- factor(
  rate_df$model,
  levels = model_names
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Create Figure
# ------------------------------------------------------------

p_age <- ggplot(
  rate_df,
  aes(
    x = band,
    y = rate,
    colour = model,
    group = model
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Logistic Regression" = "#c1666b",
      "XGBoost" = "#e08a3c",
      "TensorFlow NN" = "#2a9d8f",
      "PyTorch NN" = "#1f3a5f"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0.4, 0.75),
    breaks = seq(0.40, 0.75, by = 0.05),
    minor_breaks = seq(0.40, 0.75, by = 0.025)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Age band (years)",
    y = "Favourable-outcome rate\n(predicted non-default)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey88"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey93"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Save and Display Figure
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggsave(
  here("images", "fig_age_gradient.png"),
  plot = p_age,
  width = 7.5,
  height = 4.5,
  dpi = 300,
  bg = "white"
)

print(p_age)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================
# Figure 4.7: Four-Fifths Ratios for Sex and Age by Model
# ============================================================
# Point estimates are shown for sex and age across both datasets.
# The dashed horizontal line marks the 0.8 four-fifths screening threshold.
# Values below the threshold are treated as screening evidence of group-level
# outcome disparity rather than evidence of unlawful discrimination.


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Four-Fifths Ratio
# ------------------------------------------------------------

four_fifths_ratio <- function(
  prediction,
  group
) {

  # Favourable outcome = predicted nondefault = class 0
  rates <- tapply(
    prediction == 0,
    group,
    mean
  )

  min(
    rates,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) /
    max(
      rates,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate Four-Fifths Ratios for One Dataset
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ratios_for <- function(
  path,
  dataset_label,
  age_col,
  age_breaks,
  male_code
) {

  # Read the designated reporting-run test predictions directly
  d <- read.csv(
    here("data", path),
    check.names = FALSE
  )

  # Reconstruct the sex groups using the dataset-specific encoding
  sex_group <- ifelse(
    d$SEX == male_code,
    "male",
    "female"
  )

  # Create the same age groups used in the RQ3 analysis
  age_group <- cut(
    d[[age_col]],
    breaks = age_breaks
  )

  model_cols <- c(
    "Logistic_Regression",
    "XGBoost",
    "TensorFlow_NN",
    "PyTorch_NN"
  )

  model_names <- c(
    "Logistic Regression",
    "XGBoost",
    "TensorFlow NN",
    "PyTorch NN"
  )

  do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(
      seq_along(model_cols),
      function(i) {

        data.frame(
          dataset = dataset_label,
          model = model_names[i],
          attribute = c(
            "Sex",
            "Age"
          ),
          ratio = c(
            four_fifths_ratio(
              d[[model_cols[i]]],
              sex_group
            ),
            four_fifths_ratio(
              d[[model_cols[i]]],
              age_group
            )
          )
        )
      }
    )
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate Ratios for Both Datasets
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ff_all <- rbind(

  ratios_for(
    path = "taiwan_test_predictions.csv",
    dataset_label = "Taiwan dataset",
    age_col = "AGE",
    age_breaks = c(
      20,
      30,
      40,
      50,
      60,
      100
    ),
    male_code = 1
  ),

  ratios_for(
    path = "german_test_predictions.csv",
    dataset_label = "German dataset",
    age_col = "Age",
    age_breaks = c(
      18,
      25,
      35,
      45,
      60,
      100
    ),
    male_code = 0
  )
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Audit Values Used in Figure 4.7
# ------------------------------------------------------------

print(ff_all)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Set Plot Ordering
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ff_all$model <- factor(
  ff_all$model,
  levels = c(
    "Logistic Regression",
    "XGBoost",
    "TensorFlow NN",
    "PyTorch NN"
  ),
  labels = c(
    "LogReg",
    "XGBoost",
    "TF NN",
    "PyTorch NN"
  )
)

ff_all$attribute <- factor(
  ff_all$attribute,
  levels = c(
    "Sex",
    "Age"
  )
)

ff_all$dataset <- factor(
  ff_all$dataset,
  levels = c(
    "Taiwan dataset",
    "German dataset"
  )
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Create Figure
# ------------------------------------------------------------

p_ff <- ggplot(
  ff_all,
  aes(
    x = model,
    y = ratio,
    fill = attribute
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(
      width = 0.7
    ),
    width = 0.62
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.8,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#c1666b",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.6,
    y = 0.82,
    label = "0.8 screening threshold",
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3,
    colour = "#c1666b"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ dataset
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Sex" = "#8fbfbf",
      "Age" = "#1f3a5f"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(
      0,
      1
    ),
    breaks = seq(
      0,
      1,
      by = 0.2
    ),
    minor_breaks = seq(
      0,
      1,
      by = 0.1
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Four-fifths ratio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(
    base_size = 11
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 20,
      hjust = 1
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 11
    ),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(
      1.4,
      "lines"
    )
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Save and Display Figure
# ------------------------------------------------------------

ggsave(
  here(
    "images",
    "fig_fairness_ratios.png"
  ),
  plot = p_ff,
  width = 8.5,
  height = 4.5,
  dpi = 300,
  bg = "white"
)

print(p_ff)
```
